introduction-its-not-magic-its-math.core: S3 Intelligent-Tiering moves objects between access tiers automatically, but charges a per-object monitoring fee. It saves money only when the per-object storage savings exceed that fee, which depends on object size and access pattern.

first_principles.problem: Teams enable Intelligent-Tiering everywhere and see bills rise on buckets of small objects.
truths: Monitoring costs per object, not per GB.
derivation: Model the **storage savings per GB** when the object cools.

analogy.title: A smart thermostat with a subscription fee
analogy.story: It saves on heating, but for a tiny room the subscription costs more than the savings.
analogy.breaks: It also avoids retrieval fees for unpredictable access, which is a non-price benefit.

example.title: Two buckets
flow: Bucket A: 100 MB videos → big savings

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Enable it where the maths works.

check.q: Why can S3 Intelligent-Tiering increase costs?
check.a: Its per-object monitoring fee can exceed storage savings for small objects.

the-cost-formula.core: For each object: savings = size × (Standard price − cooler tier price) × fraction of time cooled, and cost = monitoring fee per object. It's worthwhile when savings > fee.

first_principles.problem: Without a formula, decisions are guesses.
truths: Monitoring is priced per 1,000 objects per month.
Objects cool after 30/90 days without access.

analogy.title: Is a bulk-buy club worth the fee?
analogy.story: Only if what you save on purchases exceeds the membership cost.
analogy.breaks: Prices vary by region, so plug in current rates.

example.title: One 1 MB object, cooled to IA

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: Even 1 MB objects can pay off if they cool.

check.q: What are the two variables in the S3-INT decision?
check.a: The per-object monitoring fee and the per-GB storage savings from cooler tiers (which depend on object size).

calculating-the-break-even-point.core: Break-even size = monitoring fee ÷ per-GB savings. With IA-tier savings around $0.0105/GB and a $0.0000025 fee, break-even is about 0.24 MB (~250 KB) for objects that cool. Smaller objects cost more to monitor than they save.

first_principles.problem: Teams need a concrete threshold to decide which buckets or prefixes to enable it on.
truths: The fee is constant per object.
Their intersection is the break-even point.
derivation: Adjust for the **fraction of objects that actually cool**.

analogy.title: The minimum order for free delivery
analogy.story: Below a certain basket size, the delivery fee outweighs the discount.
analogy.breaks: If objects are accessed often and never cool, there's no saving at any size.

steps.label: Rule of thumb
steps.detail: Objects above roughly 250 KB that cool are good candidates.

code.text:
fee = 0.0025 / 1000          # $ per object-month
delta = 0.023 - 0.0125        # $ per GB-month (Frequent → Infrequent)
print(fee / delta * 1024, "MB")  # ≈ 0.24 MB

check.q: How do you compute the S3-INT break-even object size?
check.a: Divide the per-object monitoring fee by the per-GB storage price saved in the cooler tier.

the-128-kb-safety-valve.core: AWS doesn't monitor or auto-tier objects smaller than 128 KB in Intelligent-Tiering. They stay in the Frequent tier at Standard price with no monitoring fee, which limits the small-object penalty but means no savings for them.

first_principles.problem: Early adopters paid monitoring fees on millions of tiny files with no possible savings.
truths: Tiny objects can never repay the fee.
AWS changed the rules to protect customers.
Below-threshold objects still use Standard pricing.
derivation: Objects **< 128 KB**: no monitoring fee, never tiered.
The 128 KB–~250 KB band still **can lose money**.

analogy.title: A store waiving the membership fee for tiny purchases
analogy.story: You don't pay the fee, but you don't get the discount either.
analogy.breaks: The threshold reduces losses but doesn't create savings for small files.

check.q: What happens to objects under 128 KB in S3 Intelligent-Tiering?
check.a: They aren't monitored or charged the fee, and they always stay in the Frequent Access tier.

fleet-level-analysis-thinking-at-scale.core: Decide per bucket or prefix using the object size distribution and access patterns (S3 Storage Lens, Inventory): sum the expected savings minus fees across all objects, and target lifecycle or Intelligent-Tiering rules by prefix.

first_principles.problem: A bucket mixes huge videos with millions of tiny thumbnails, and a blanket decision is wrong for half of it.
truths: Inventory reports give the size distribution.
Rules can be scoped by prefix, tag or size.
derivation: Export **S3 Inventory** (size, storage class, last modified).
Analyse the **size histogram and access** (Storage Lens, CloudTrail data events).

analogy.title: Pricing a mixed warehouse
analogy.story: Bulky furniture belongs in cheap long-term storage; small fast-moving items stay near the front.
analogy.breaks: Access patterns change, so re-analyse periodically.

check.q: Why analyse S3 Inventory before enabling Intelligent-Tiering?
check.a: Buckets mix object sizes and access patterns, and only the distribution shows where the savings exceed the fees.
